reasoning: Very close. Both outputs converge on the same correct headline diagnosis (the flow asks twice and returns nothing before screen 3), and both handle the evidential poverty honestly rather than faking observation. A wins on the two axes that matter most for this task: completeness of the diagnosis, and the quality of the instrument it hands back for resolving uncertainty. A finds four substantive problems B never reaches -- the real screen count is 4-6 because email signup implies a verification interstitial and an app exit to the mail client (M1, and A's first-person cold read in section 3 is what surfaces it: the highest-stall moment in the walkthrough is a screen the user did not know they had, which is a direct, specific answer to 'I cannot say what'); the abandonment/resume semantics and where the account record is written (M5); a 3-screens-x-5-states = 15-cell coverage matrix with the four states that actually occur named (M6); and a 'what must not change' section that pre-empts the four most common wrong fixes (merge into one scroll, add a product tour, delete a genuine seeding step, bolt on guest mode). On the flagged criterion -- converting findings into testable predictions -- A's instrument is stronger: each catch carries a countable artifact, a specific check, AND the conditional consequence of each outcome ('if skippable, B1 drops Blocker to Major'; 'if A3 and A5 are both false, the top three findings collapse'), plus a funnel prediction explicitly recorded so it can be scored later. B gives a prior and a 10-minute test per row, which is good, but rarely says what each result does to the verdict. A also commits harder without overclaiming: it issues a verdict and three Blockers while stating LOW confidence and tagging every pixel-dependent item [needs build], where B softens everything to 'candidate diagnosis, do not treat as a verified defect'. B is genuinely better in two respects and the gap is narrow: its section 6 copy rewrites are the most directly shippable output in either document (literal strings, error-message rewrites, CTA alternatives, a localization sizing note), and its section 2 weight budget is a fill-in-the-blank instrument that converts 'heavy' into eight countable numbers -- arguably the best-targeted single artifact relative to the user's stated inability to name the problem. B also raises a measurement trap A misses entirely (do not evaluate these changes on signup completion; a 20% signup lift with a 25% activation drop looks like a win on the dashboard you would naturally check), and its refusal to fabricate a WCAG audit while still naming the four SCs most likely to fail is exemplary. B is the leaner, more consumable document. A pays for its extra ~107 lines with real process exhaust -- an unrequested ~55-line provisional targets doc, a scorecard scored against criteria A itself invented, and findings-cap bookkeeping -- and buries its best entry point (the ordered action plan) at section 12. That cost is real but cosmetic against A's diagnostic breadth. Both pass all four expectations; A is ahead on expectations 1 and 2, B on expectation 4, tie on 3.

strengths: Catches that the flow is not three screens: email signup implies a verification interstitial plus an app exit to the mail client, making the real count 4-6. The single best answer to 'I cannot say what', and absent from B entirely

First-person cold read (section 3) walks the actual described screens in order with stall ratings, which is what produces the uncounted-screen finding -- the most concrete engagement with the specific flow in either document
Conditional severity throughout: each finding states what each test outcome does to the verdict ('if skippable, B1 drops Blocker to Major'), not just what to test
Records a falsifiable prediction ('the largest single drop is at screen 2 or the verification exit, not at signup') explicitly so it can be scored later
The B1 seeding-step-vs-preferences-step fork with a 60-second field-overlap discriminator against Settings: a genuine either/or where the fix inverts, resolved by a free check

Covers system-level ground B misses: abandonment resume point and where the account record is written (M5), and a 15-cell state matrix naming the four states that actually occur -- email already registered, expired verification link, offline mid-signup, slow dashboard first load (M6)
Section 8 'what must not change' guards against the four most common wrong fixes, including the product tour and the merge-into-one-scroll

Honest about evidence at finding granularity: [needs build] tags, 'I saw zero of three screens', and an explicit note that its own provisional targets are invented and the scorecard is circular until overwritten
Section 12 sequences the actions cheapest-check-first, so the user spends nothing before the highest-value ambiguity is resolved
Stress test names A5 as load-bearing for three of nine catches and admits the scope gate scored 4/5 on inference rather than inspection
weaknesses: Roughly 80 of its ~107 extra lines over B are low-yield process material: an unrequested ~55-line provisional targets document, findings-cap bookkeeping ('9 against the ~12 cap', 'Truncated: none')
Section 4's scorecard scores the flow against criteria A wrote itself in section 11 -- a closed loop that adds little beyond what section 5 already says
Internal vocabulary a reader has no context for: 'Pass 0/2/4', review-passes.md, the calibration log, 'the 4.07:1 defect'
B3 ('nothing designed to produce a feeling') is a meta-finding about a missing design contract rather than a defect in the flow; calling it a Blocker inflates severity
Fixes are clear directions but rarely specified to the string or field level -- less turnkey than B's copy tables
The most useful section (the ordered action plan) sits at line 345, after everything else

strengths: Section 2 weight budget: eight fill-in metrics with targets that convert the felt sense into countable numbers, plus the instruction to test in incognito with autofill off. The best-targeted artifact in either document relative to 'I cannot say what'

Section 6 copy rewrites are the most directly shippable output in either document -- literal after-strings, two error-message rewrites, a CTA alternatives table, and a localization note about 30% expansion in German and French
Ten candidate diagnoses each with an explicit prior and a 10-minute test the user can run themselves
The 'three screens built by three people in three design dialects' alternative hypothesis, with a 2-minute side-by-side canvas test -- A only touches this obliquely
Section 9 refuses to fabricate a WCAG audit, explains why a fabricated audit is worse than none, then still delivers value by naming the four SCs most likely to fail (1.4.3, 3.3.2, 2.4.7, 2.5.5)
Stress test point 4 raises a trap A never mentions: do not measure these changes on signup completion; a 20% signup lift with a 25% activation drop looks like a win
Cleanest structure of the two -- limits, answer, measure, diagnose, fix, pushback, copy, stress test -- with the framing up front and the answer in section 1
Flags its own sharpest objection loudly ('answer question 1 before touching R2') rather than leaving it buried in a counter-cases section
weaknesses: Misses the uncounted verification screen and app exit entirely, which is the likeliest single source of unnameable weight in an email-signup flow
Section 3's table is labelled 'ranked' but its order contradicts its own severity column: D5 is Critical/High yet sits below D3 and D4, both Major
No coverage of resumability, where the account record is written, or systematic empty/loading/error/offline state coverage
Section 7 (visual hierarchy) is the closest thing in either document to restating usability principles -- 'exactly one element should win the 2-second test'
Section 6 is the largest section and rewrites copy it has never seen; honestly marked as reconstruction, but its value is contingent on the user's actual strings matching the pattern
Softer commitment: 'do not treat any row as a verified defect' is correct but stops short of A's verdict-with-stated-confidence, and priors rarely carry a stated consequence for the verdict
Only two guardrails against wrong fixes (section 5), versus A's four -- notably nothing warning against the product tour or the merge-into-one-long-scroll
